title: Okafor v St Aldhelm's Hospital NHS Trust

summary.text: Acting for Daniel Okafor (claimant), this brief addresses 3 issue(s) arising from Okafor v St Aldhelm's Hospital NHS Trust: Mr Okafor wants to claim damages in negligence for the failure to warn him of a material risk and of the alternative treatment before he consented to surgery.
Did St Aldhelm's Hospital NHS Trust breach the duty to warn Daniel Okafor of material risks and reasonable alternatives before consent was given? Favourable for Daniel Okafor.
Did the clinician's conduct fall below the standard of a responsible body of medical opinion? Finely balanced for Daniel Okafor.
Can Daniel Okafor prove that the breach caused the harm, on the but-for test or a modified approach? Unfavourable for Daniel Okafor.

facts.text: On 2 February 2024 Mr Okafor consulted Mr Lyle about chronic neck pain radiating into his left arm.

Mr Lyle recommended cervical decompression surgery. He did not mention the roughly 2 per cent risk of damage to the nerve root supplying the hand, and he did not mention the alternative of a further six months of physiotherapy and steroid injections.
During the consultation Mr Okafor told Mr Lyle that his career depended on fine finger control of his left hand.
Mr Okafor signed a consent form and the operation took place on 11 April 2024. It was performed with proper skill.
The risk of nerve damage materialised. Mr Okafor has permanently lost fine motor control in two fingers of his left hand and can no longer perform professionally.

Mr Okafor says that if he had been warned of the risk he would not have consented to surgery on that date but would have tried physiotherapy first and sought a second opinion. He accepts he might eventually have had the same operation.

The Trust relies on evidence from two surgeons that many responsible spinal surgeons in 2024 did not routinely mention a 2 per cent risk to patients, and argues that the surgery itself was not negligent so the failure to warn caused no loss.

issues.question: Did St Aldhelm's Hospital NHS Trust breach the duty to warn Daniel Okafor of material risks and reasonable alternatives before consent was given?

proposition.text: On policy grounds, causation may be established by a narrow modification of traditional principles in order to vindicate the patient's right of autonomy and to give effect to the duty to warn of material risks before consent to surgery.

A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would be likely to attach significance to it, or if the doctor is or should reasonably be aware that this particular patient would attach significance to it.

opposing_precedents.case_name: Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee

proposition.text: The Bolam test measures a professional against the standard of a responsible body of practitioners in the same field.

issues.question: Can Daniel Okafor prove that the breach caused the harm, on the but-for test or a modified approach?

opposing_precedents.case_name: Barnett v Chelsea and Kensington Hospital Management Committee

proposition.text: The but-for test: the claimant must prove on the balance of probabilities that, but for the defendant's breach, the damage would not have occurred.

opposing_precedents.case_name: Wilsher v Essex Area Health Authority

proposition.text: Showing that a breach added one more possible cause to several existing ones, or materially increased the risk among distinct agents, does not discharge the burden of proving causation.
